description: The golden chanterelle is a choice edible mushroom with a yellow-to-orange funnel-shaped cap and decurrent, blunt, fork-like ridges (false gills) running down a tapering stipe. It is ectomycorrhizal, fruiting from soil in association with trees, and is prized worldwide for its firm texture and faintly fruity (apricot-like) aroma.
edibilityNotes: A prized choice edible, but must always be cooked thoroughly; raw or undercooked chanterelles can cause gastrointestinal upset. Only eat after positively distinguishing from the toxic jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) and the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis) by confirming the blunt, fork-like false gills (ridges), not true sharp-edged gills.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, North America, and parts of Asia. Note: many regional populations once called C. cibarius are now recognized as distinct species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus olearius (jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic. Has true, sharp-edged gills (not blunt ridges), grows in dense clusters on wood or buried roots rather than singly from soil, and is more uniformly orange. Causes severe GI illness (muscarine-like / illudin toxins).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (false chanterelle)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Has true, thin, repeatedly forked gills that are more orange than the cap, a softer texture, and lacks the fruity aroma. Generally regarded as poor or mildly upsetting rather than a choice edible.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus illudens (eastern jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic North American counterpart. True gills, clustered on wood, contains illudin S; gills are bioluminescent in fresh specimens. Causes severe GI illness.
